thread.title: Would you pay for a phoneless vacation? Travel companies now offer this as a perk

author: Kari Paul
title: Would you pay for a phoneless vacation? Travel companies now offer this as a perk
text:
To truly enjoy time off, first you must put your phone down — but people can’t seem to do it. 
“Vacation can provide the quantity of time that quality relationships require,” Katie Denis, vice president of American Project: Time Off, a nonprofit aimed at breaking stigmas against taking vacation. “But if you are vacationing with your job, you’re missing out on the benefits that travel provides.”
Now you can pay someone else to do it for you. The newly-launched travel company Off The Grid offers group trips with itineraries, lodging, and a daily breakfast included — and no phones allowed. Other resorts and getaways are advertising themselves as phone-free as well. Punta Placer, a beach resort in Mexico, is completely “off the grid” without Wi-Fi or phones for $90 a night. 
OARS adventure company uses its location in Idaho’s “River of No Return,” which has no cell service , as a selling point. Many yoga and meditation retreats, including Dhamma Dhara Vipassana Meditation Center in Massachusetts and the worldwide locations of Vipassana meditation retreats, also have no-phone rules. 
If the social pressure doesn’t help, the money they’re paying for the privilege of a phoneless vacation will. The yoga retreats cost anything from $550 for eight days in Portugal to $9,000 for seven days in Thailand . The 10-day Off The Grid trips range from $1,500 for a tour of Lisbon, Portugal to $1,650 for the trip to Prague. The cost is slightly higher than the average Groupon deal for travel: A comparable one-person trip to Lisbon listed on the site is $850 while a 10-day tour for two is $1,800 . 
All of the existing trips are sold out, Beattie said, and more were added for later in 2018. Attendees include everyone from college students and millennials to people in their 60s who want to get away from phones. 
People appear to be desperate to kick their smartphone addiction. Just 37% of travelers unplug completely when taking time off, a study released Thursday from Alamo Rent A Car found -- a significant drop from 53% that unplugged in 2017. More than half of people say they put pressure on themselves to work on vacation. This trend comes despite numerous studies that show tech is ruining the way we communicate and relax. 
Some hotels are charging extra for the amenity of unplugging. The Mandarin Oriental New York lets luxury hotel guests check their phones in for an “unplugged retreat,” during which they take classes in mindful journaling and meditation. Phones are cleaned and polished before being returned to guests after the digital detox. 
The Four Seasons Costa Rica lets visitors turn their phones into the front desk, according to Travel + Leisure, and if they make it 24 hours without the device, they win an Apple iPhone AAPL, +0.35% case. 
“We wanted to build an experience that took pressure off people to always be plugged in and allow them to reclaim their time — even if it’s just once or twice a year,” Off the Grid co-founder Zach Beattie told MarketWatch. When guests arrive, they all unplug together, turning their phones off and “setting an intention” for the week before putting them away in a basic cloth pouch for the duration of the 10-day trip. 
They are then provided with a “dumb phone” — a simple Motorola MSI, +0.59% device without internet access that only makes and receives phone calls, with emergency numbers pre-programmed, as well as a notebook and a disposable camera. Beattie’s company launched in January.
Many travelers simply don’t have the self control to force themselves off social media and work emails. Some 16% of people polled by Alamo Rent A Car said they could “never unplug” from social media during a vacation and 43% said they wish they could. 
Although travelers could at any time technically rifle through their bags and turn on their smartphones or hidden tablet, Beattie said the phoneless peer pressure of the trip is meant to keep them on track. “We cater to people who want to have a highly-interactive experience with other travelers.” That way, people are looking at their surroundings and no one has their nose buried in a phone.
